title: Conquer yourself
hook: one who conquers himself is greater than one who conquers a thousand men in battle (Dhammapada 103)
tomorrow: how does a jar get full when the tap only drips?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one word of peace: a few true words, said when they can land. Zoe sent one line. Theo wrote back: coffee, Sunday.

Sports finals, award shows, a debate clip everyone is sharing: winners get crowned all the time. But what's the biggest win a person can have? The Dhammapada answers with a battlefield. In Max Müller's translation: "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors." And the suttas tell of a man with a sword who had to learn to stop.
screen: `WINNERS GET CROWNED ALL THE TIME.` → `A THOUSAND TIMES A THOUSAND.` → `THE ONE WHO CONQUERS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: In the Majjhima Nikaya, a bandit named Angulimala terrorizes the countryside. People warn the Buddha off the road. He walks it anyway. Angulimala grabs his sword and runs after him, and can't catch him, though the Buddha is only walking. He shouts: stop, monk! The Buddha answers: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. I've stopped harming, he explains; you haven't. The bandit throws his sword away and asks to become a monk. That's this path's question for today, and Buddhism's answer: the real victory is over your own mind. Not the self erased; the self tamed, the way a rider trains a horse. Now a neighbor who says something close, in its own words. The Book of Proverbs, scripture for Jews and Christians: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Shared: ruling yourself outranks taking a city. And the honest difference. Proverbs sets self-rule inside reverence for God; the same book says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The Buddha's verse calls on no creator. The tamed mind is a step toward nibbana. Two houses, one battlefield inside, and different reasons for fighting there.
screen: `ANGULIMALA RUNS, AND CAN'T CATCH UP.` · `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` · `PROVERBS: RULE YOUR SPIRIT.` · `ONE BATTLE, DIFFERENT REASONS.` · then, large: `CONQUER MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and sit still. Soon an urge will come: to scratch, to shift, to check the phone, to finish an argument in your head. When it comes, notice it, name it softly, and don't follow it for three breaths. One small battle, won without a fight.
Conquer yourself: the greater victory, over your own mind, said in the Dhammapada and, in its own way, in Proverbs.
Carry this: conquer myself, the only battle I can win alone. Six verses in, and the sword's on the ground.

howItsDone: Buddhists describe training the mind as taming it, through meditation and the precepts; Jewish and Christian readers of Proverbs speak of ruling one's spirit, slow to anger, within reverence for God.

chat.meaning: Dhammapada 103: conquering yourself beats conquering a thousand times a thousand. Angulimala's win was stopping, not winning.
